query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the average grain size in the FeNiCrCoCu high‐entropy alloy coating (via a controlled pre-annealing process) will reduce the fraction of high-energy grain boundaries active at high temperatures, thereby suppressing grain-boundary sliding and dynamic recrystallization. This promotes a deformation mode dominated by bulk dislocation glide, ultimately resulting in lower wear rates and a more uniform microscopic deformation during high-temperature sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: Thin FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with a baseline fine-grained microstructure on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: Apply a pre-annealing treatment to induce controlled grain growth (increasing the grain size relative to the baseline condition).
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime (e.g., temperatures >400 °C with a controlled sliding velocity and load).
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary density (i.e., the average grain size), which controls the activation of grain-boundary sliding and dynamic recrystallization processes.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, fine-grained coatings tend to activate grain-boundary sliding and dynamic recrystallization, which localize deformation and increase wear. By increasing the grain size, the overall grain-boundary area is reduced, thus limiting these thermally activated, boundary-mediated deformation processes and shifting the response towards more homogeneous dislocation glide.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline fine-grained state, the coarser-grained coating is predicted to show a reduction in wear volume (improved wear resistance) and exhibit a more uniform deformation pattern with fewer localized grain-boundary sliding features under high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.baseline: The standard coating with a fine-grained microstructure (as originally applied without the pre-annealing grain growth treatment).
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be dominant under high-temperature sliding conditions (>400 °C) where thermal activation of grain-boundary sliding and dynamic recrystallization occur. At lower temperatures, alternative mechanisms may prevail and the effect of grain size on wear resistance might be less pronounced.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of wear reduction and the shift in deformation mode depend on the degree of grain growth and potential competing effects such as oxidation or phase instability that may arise at high temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coating samples on identical metal substrates. One set remains in the baseline fine-grained state while the other set undergoes a controlled pre-annealing treatment to achieve coarser grains. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding tests (e.g., at >400 °C under constant load and sliding speed). Use in situ wear measurement methods and post-test microscopy to assess wear volume and microscopic deformation features.
measurements: Microscopic characterization of deformation modes (e.g., SEM/EBSD to assess grain-boundary sliding signs and dynamic recrystallization)
Grain size distribution before and after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coarser-grained samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear volume and/or if they exhibit similar or more pronounced localized deformation (e.g., grain-boundary sliding or dynamic recrystallization features) compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis—that controlled grain growth enhances wear resistance via suppression of grain-boundary mediated deformation—is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 , whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol −1 . Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M 23 C 6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion. frame.system: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy applied as a thin coating (with a defined microstructure and baseline composition) on a conventional metal substrate intended for high-temperature sliding applications.
frame.goal: To understand and explain the mechanistic link between microstructural evolution (such as grain-boundary behavior or phase stability) during sliding and the resulting overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation in the high-temperature regime.
frame.limitation: There is currently a lack of a single, predictive mechanistic explanation that directly links controlled microstructural modifications or compositional variations in the coating with directional wear resistance and deformation behavior under high-temperature sliding conditions.
